claims.text: High-load cyclic service causes a formerly single-phase high-entropy alloy to undergo localized deformation-induced transformation into a secondary brittle phase.
The service-induced secondary phase may be an ordered intermetallic such as B2.
The secondary phase preferentially nucleates at crack tips, grain boundaries, and regions of high dislocation density.
Formation of the secondary phase restricts dislocation movement away from crack tips.
Restricting dislocation movement near crack tips diminishes crack blunting or shielding and lowers fracture resistance.
Dislocation channels that permit movement away from a crack tip can contribute to high toughness.
The initial material is a homogeneous, typically FCC, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The initial single-phase alloy has high intrinsic toughness and ductility.
Severe mechanical loading produces dislocation accumulation and mechanical twinning.
Dislocation accumulation and mechanical twinning provide nucleation sites for the proposed brittle-phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism causes a ductile-to-brittle transition.
High-stress cyclic loading will measurably reduce fracture toughness relative to an ambient, low-load control.
High-stress cyclic loading will change fracture morphology from ductile dimples to brittle cleavage facets.
Loaded specimens will contain newly formed secondary-phase regions at locations formerly supporting dislocation channels.
The transformation and toughness loss occur only after a critical cyclic load, strain, or temperature threshold is exceeded.
At moderate loads and ambient temperature, the alloy retains its single-phase microstructure and toughness.

Failure to detect a significant secondary phase together with statistically equivalent toughness in loaded and control specimens would falsify the proposed transformation-mediated embrittlement mechanism.
